Number of elephants in the country 
†4702. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the number of elephants is declining rapidly in the country; 
(b) if so, the figures of number of elephants during the last five years; 
(c) the major steps taken by Government in this regard keeping in view the 
decreasing number of elephants; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The 
estimated population of elephants in the country has shown an increase from 
25,877 in 1997 to 26,413 in 2002 when the last census was carried out. 
(c) and (d) Elephants have been included in Schedule 1 of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 which prohibits their hunting and also trade in ivory. Export 
of ivory from the country is also banned. India is a signatory to the Convention on 
International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna & Flora (CITES) which 
prohibits international trade in ivory and other elephant products. Government of 
India provides financial assistance under Project Elephant to major elephant-
bearing states in the country for protection of elephants and their habitats and also 
for mitigating human-elephant conflict An amount of Rs. 13.34 Cr. was released 
under the Project during 2004-05. 25 Elephant Reserves have been notified in 
the country for the systematic and focused management of elephants. 
Government of India has also empowered the C.B.I, under the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute the wildlife offenders.

Statement-II 
Action taken Report 
Rural Drinking Water supply is a State subject. Government of India 
introduced the centrally sponsored Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP) in 1972-1973 to accelerate coverage of problem 
villages by rendering financial and technical assistance to States. The entire 
programme was given a mission approach when the National Drinking Water 
Mission (NDWM) was set up in 1986. NDWM was renamed as Rajiv Gandhi 
National Drinking Water Mission (RGNDWM) in 1991. 
2. The primary objective of RGNDWM was to improve the performance and 
cost effectiveness of the on-going programmes in the field of rural drinking 
water supply and sanitation and help ensure availability of adequate quanity of 
drinking water of acceptable quality on a long-term basis. 
3. Rural Drinking Water Supply is largely dependent on ground water (85%). 
Though ground water is less susceptible to pollution as compared to surface water, 
it is affected by the composition of eath's crust. Leaching action of the Arsenic 
bearing rocks at some places leads to occurrence of Arsenic in ground water. 
4. Contamination of ground water with Arsenic was first noticed in 6 
districts in West Bengal in the early 1980s. The first attempt to tackle the 
problem was made in 1988 by sanctioning an investigative study under the R&D 
programmes. Thereafter, several R&D projects as well as field-oriented 
programmes, were sanctioned in the Arsenic affected areas. 
5. At the instance of RGNDWM, the States carried out a survey of quality-
affected habitations in 1991 based on 1% random sampling. As per results of 
this survey, 3,133 habitations in West Bengal were found to be affected with 
arsenic contamination. Another survey in 2 phases was ordered in the year 2000, 
based on 5 to 10% stratified sampling of sources in each Block in Phase-I, 
followed by Phase-ll in which 100% testing of sources was done in the Blocks 
where quality affected sources were found in the Phase I. The West Bengal 
government has reported 4,973 habitations affected with arsenic contamination in 
75 blocks in 8 districts, namely, 24 Parganas South, 24 Parganas North, Malda, 
Nadia, Bardawan, Murshidabad, Hoogly and Howrah. The total population at 
risk in these 75 blocks of 8 districts is estimated as 16 million. 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
6. Among the various techniques developed for removal of arsenic, two methods, viz., (i) 
Co-precipitation technique and (ii) Absorption technique, are the most common. The PHED, 
Government of West Bengal and other organization like. All India Institute of Hygiene and 
Public Health (AIIH&PH), Calcutta and Bengal College of Engineering, Howrah have also 
installed arsenic removal plants in the Arsenic affected aeras of the State. Besides, Domestic 
filters have also been developed by these organizations. A programme of Water Quality 
Monitoring an Surveillance was also launched by RGNDWM by initially setting up State and 
District level Water Quality Testing laboratories to ensure providing safe drinking water 
by the State Governments and generate awareness about water quality among rural 
masses. 17 district laboratories were sanctioned by RGNDWM for West Bengal, out of 
which 13 were established. In the remaining 6 districts, the State Government established 
laboratories from their own sources. One Mobile laboratory was also sanctioned by 
RGNDWM and delivered to West Bengal Government. , 
7. Helping State Governments to tackle water-quality problems in the rural areas is 
one of the objectives of the RGNDWM. Sub-mission programmes were introduced 
in 1992-93 to tackle water quality and sustainability problems. The funding pattern was 
75:25 between Centre and State. Under the Sub-mission programme for control of Arsenic, 
four projects proposed by the State Government were sanctioned during 1994-98 for 
West Bengal by RGNDWM. The West Bengal Government implemented these projects.

Territories through the Appropriate Authorities appointed under the Act at State,

Revival of Malaria 
4728. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that reappearance of mosquitoes through out the country 
has resulted in revival of Malaria; 
(b) whether Government have conducted any research on Malaria repellants 
like planting of Marigold flowers or other such measures; if so, the details 
thereof; 
(c) whether inadequate sewerage in cities and towns is one of the factors for 
reappearance of mosquitoes and revival of Malaria; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken do deal with the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The mosquito nuisance is 
determined by several factors like unplanned urbanization, physical 
environment, life style of the people and water-management system. There are 
several species of the mosquitoes which have different breeding habits. The 
mosquito for spread of malaria i.e. 'Anopheles' usually breeds in clean water. The 
effective control of mosquito can be achieved by environmental modifications & 
manipulations. The National Malaria control Programme was started by the Govt, 
of India in 1953 which was converted to National Malaria Eradication Programme 
in 1958. There was spectacular reduction of malaria incidence as well as deaths. 
However, during late 1970's there was resurgence of malaria due to operational, 
technical and administrative factors. With the introduction of Modified Plan of 
Operation in 1977, the number of malaria cases declined from 6.4 million to 
below 2 million in 2002. Since then the number of cases of malaria has 
remained below 2 million. 
(b) Though there are some reports in literature about the insecticidal 
and repellent activity of the extracts of Tagetus (Marigold), these have not 
been used/studied as malaria repellent by planting of Marigold flowers and 
other plants in the country. 
There is however a report on a study conducted by scientists from Kenya 
and Ethiopia on live potted plants including Tagetus (Marigold) tested as mosquito 
repellent which did not show any significant repellent effect of Tagetus. 
(c) and (d) Bad sewerage system cause breeding of Culex mosquitoes 
151 
 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
but malaria transmitting Anopheles mosquitoes do not breed in sewer water. 
The Govt, of India has a well defined Programme viz. National Vector Borne 
Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) for control of malaria in the country 
adopting strategies which include surveillance, early diagnosis and prompt 
treatment of cases, sustainable vector control including Indoor Residual Spray 
with insecticides treated bednets, use of larvivorous fish etc. besides Training 
& Information, Education and Communication to enlist community 
involvement. Urban Malaria Scheme is also being implemented in 131 Towns 
in the country to reduce density of mosquitoes and to prevent spread of malaria.

4773. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to

(a) whether over utilisation of Railway Tracks to the extent of 125 per cent would

cent to 90 per cent in the Southern Railway;

(e) whether among the railway accidents, it is found that human failure is the highest, 
and the special measures undertaken to curb this kind of failures? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) No, Sir. Over utilization of sectional capacity in some case may lead to 
some what less availability of track for maintenance. However, safety of track is not 
allowed to be affected and in case of need suitable temporary speed restrictions are 
imposed to ensure safety, 
(b) Sometimes, coaches and wagons rejected by Neutral Control Examiner 
(NCE) on account of not carrying out certain modifications, leaving minor deficiencies in 
scale of passenger amenities which do not affect safety, are permitted to be deployed for 
service. Such permission is given judiciously, so as not to detain rolling stock after overhaul 
in workshops, in the interest of overall availability of coaches and wagons for public use. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) Yes, Sir. Safety is the prime concern of Indian Railways ana adoption of new 
measures to improve safety is a continuous process. The measures being taken by Indian 
Railways to minimize incidence of accidents include adoption of suitable modern 
technology for interlocking and signaling systems, up-gradation of track and rolling 
stock, modernization of maintenance practices, replacement of over aged assets, up-
gradation of training aids like simulators, checks on observance of safety precautions and 
provision of Anti Collision Device with continuous and sustained efforts, the number of 
accidents are coming down over the years.

Steel Prices 
4793. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
SHRI MATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Tata Steel has hiked its long-term contract prices 
by 20 per cent effective from April 1,2005; 
(b) if so, whether other PSUs and Joint Sector Steel Plants are likely to follow 
suit; 
212 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the impact of rise in steel prices on Indian Economy and common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) No, Sir. 
With effect from April 1, 2005 Tata Steel has increased the prices of its 
different products by 8-12%. 
(b) and (c) With effect from April 1,2005 Steel Authority of India Limited 
(SAIL) has increased prices of its different products by 6-9% and Rashtriya Ispat 
Nigam Limited (RINL) has increased its prices by 5-6%. The price increase has 
been attributed to the increase in cost of raw materials and strong market 
conditions. 
(d) While there are many institutional factors, which impact the growth otthe 
National Economy, the rising prices of steel, which is mainly used in the 
infrastructure and manufacturing sectors, have not inhibited growth in these 
sectors. During 2002-03, when steel prices registered an average growth of 19% 
over the previous year, the growth in capital formation in steel related segments 
of Construction, Manufacturing, Transport, Storage and Communication and 
Electricity, Gas and Water was 10.42%. 
The rise in steel prices has led to a number of representations from the 
consumer industries. In particular the construction sector, which uses about 
60% of steel produced in the country,  has strongly represented against the 
increase in prices.

Steel production 
4795. SHRIS. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to refer to 
unstarred Question 607 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 4th March, 2005 and state: 
(a) the details of concrete plan to achieve the target of steel production by over 100 
million tonnes per annum by 2020; 
(b) whether the iron ore reserves of the country are sufficient to meet the target; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the steps proposed to be taken thereon; and 
(d) the role assigned to public sector steel companies in achieving the target 
particularly to Salem Steel Plant? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) The proposed 
National Steel Policy envisages an indigenous production of over 100 million tonnes of 
steel by 2019-20 and seeks to remove the supply-side constraints to the growth of this 
industry in an open, globally integrated and competitive environment in order to achieve the 
goal. After 
214

the Policy is approved, a concrete action plan to achieve the given targets 
is expected to be prepared by an empowered Group of Ministers under the 
Chairmanship of the Steel Minister. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) It is estimated that 190 million tonnes of iron ore would be required 
for producing 110 million tonnes of steel by 2019-20. Additional mining 
capacity would be developed to ensure availability of the required quantity 
of iron ore. 
(d) The proposed NSP seeks to remove bottlenecks towards achieving 
the level of growth envisaged by 20 19-20 for the steel sector. While it 
addresses the constraints for growth in the different segments of the steel 
industry, it does not specify growth targets at the plant level.

welcoming this Bill. I had welcomed it most wholeheartedly when it was first 
brought before the House and I am very happy that the hon. Minister has taken 
the earliest opportunity to present the Bill again to this august House for its 
consideration and approval. Many distinguished speakers,

who spoke before me, spoke about the greatness of this institution. May I say 
that, in my student days, when there were only 21 Universities in the whole of 
India, we had always heard the name of the Allahabad University as topping the 
list of 21. The great Vice-Chancellors of this University, like Amarnath Jha, and 
great scholars, like Ishwari Prasad, were know to students far deep south in 
kerala, when I was a student in my University. But it is also a fact that this 
University lived far too long on its past of glory and during the last quarter of a 
century, at least, 15-20 years, it had been on the decline. Politicisation not only 
at the students level but also at the teachers level, total neglect of research 
and inability to produce men of excellence in various disciplines, which it used 
to do in the past, all these have brought down the reputation if this great University 
and it was delegated to the list of mediocre Universities in this country. That is why 
people like me wholeheartedly welcomed it when the Bill came before the House 
with the hope that a great institution with a great past and a redoubtable future 
could be retrieved from the morass into which it had fallen and made again a 
Centre of Excellence. The Bills is to declare this institution as a Centre of 
National Importance. 
I would like to make three or four points. Before I do that, may I know how 
many minutes are allotted to me? 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: You have got three minutes. 
DR. C.P. ALEXANDER: Agreat discipline that I have learnt after coming to the 
House is to convey ones views within three or four minutes. If I need one or two 
minutes more, I will crave you indulgence. 
The first point that I would like to make is that there should be some criteria 
for accepting further Universities or institutions as Centres of National Importance. I 
am not disputing the claim of the Patna Univesity which was pressed by one 
honb'le member nor am I disputing the claims of other institutions which may 
come up for the consideration of the Minister. But it is necessary that the Ministry 
should lay down some criteria or guidelines for the recognition of an institution as 
a Centre of National Importance. Some Hon'ble members who spoke before 
me.talked about autonomy for universities. But it should be understood that 
when an institution is taken up as a centre of national importance, we should 
allow the Central Government to have a say in its management and the 
ideologies, objectives and programmes on which it should place importance in 
future, so it would be good if the Central Government, that is the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development, has a common Act for all Central universities, 
instead of having separate Acts for each university, as it is today. There is the 
Banaras University; there is the Pondicherry University and there are many 
other

The third point is about the selection of the Vice-Chancellor. The existing

interview the candidates who are recommended by the selection panel. If

paper. They would all have Ph.D. degrees; they would all. have published 
books; they would all have guided research and they would all have done 
25 to 30 years of teaching. Unless you interview a candidate at some level

At some level of the se lection process, to asse ss the suitability of the

decision where on person is selected. 
Finally, the Allahabad University should turn out to be a real national 
institution. While it has been nurtured by the State of Uttar Pradesh and it

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Meningococcal Disease 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): Sir. meningococcal disease is an acute bacterial disease 
caused by the bacterium Meningococcus and is manifested by sudden 
onset of fever, severe headache, nausea and vomiting, stiff neck and 
frequently a petechial rash with pink  macules and very rarely vesicles 
often accompanied by delirium and coma. Occasionally, fulminating cases 
exhibit severe sudden prostration, ecchymoses and shock at onset. The 
causative agent at present is known to have 12 serogroups. Serogroups 
A, B, C are the commonest and have epidemic potential. Other serogroups 
to name a few W-135, Z, Y, Z etc. are less virulent. 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
A small proportion of case progress to invasive disease characterised by one 
or more clinical syndromes including bacteraemia. Many with septicaemia 
develop petechial rash. Joints may also be involved. Meningococcaemia 
may occur without meningitis. Out of 25 cases test at the National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases, Delhi, 5 cases have been found positive for 
serigroup a Meningococcal infection. 
As per the information received from the Government of NCT, a total number 
of 91 cases and 14 deaths have been reported till yesterday. Till today, there are 
111 cases and 15 deaths have occurred till today. 
The community is advised to report to the nearest health facility as soon as 
possible if there is sudden rise of high fever along with headache, vomiting, neck 
pain or skin rashes. All major hospitals such as Dr. RML Hospital, Safdarjung 
Hospital, Smt. Sucheta kriplani Hospital, Kalawati Saran Children Hospital, 
AIIMS, LNJP Hospital, G.T.B. Hospital. Hindu Rao Hospital, Deen Dayal 
Upadhyay Hospital, etc., are fully equipped to treat such patients. Hospitals in 
Delhi as well as private practitioners have been advised to notify suspected cases 
to the medical Officer, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (Telephone No. 2393 6101). 
There is no need of panic since the disease is amenable to antibiotic treatment and 
there are sufficient stocks of medicines. Facilities for rapid diagnosis of the 
disease are available at NICD. Ac ontrol room at NICD (Telephone No. 
23981289) will receive the clinical samples round the clock. Guidelines for 
prevention of disease transmission including chemoprophylaxis have been 
provided to concerned health authorities in consultation with WHO. 
The situation is under control and is being regularly monitored.

DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, I understand the concerns of not only 
the hon. Members but also the general public. I once again want to inform 
the House, through you, that we are looking at the situation and monitoring 
it very carefully. The Central and the State machinery are in full gear in 
these areas. We are carrying out surveys, monitoring and educating the 
public about how we could prevent this. A lot of measures have been taken 
to educate the people through print and electronic media and through 
loudspeakers in various parts of Delhi. At the same time, we do not want 
to create panic among the people. This is not an epidemic-like situation 
today. An epidemic occurred last in Delhi was 20 years ago. 
Now, I come to the queries raised by the hon. Members. Shri 
Narayanasamy mentioned about the short supply of medicines. There are 
two things in this. One is medicine and the other is vaccine. Vaccine is 
for prevention and medicines are for treatment. There is no short supply of 
medicines. Simple antibiotics can treat this. This is just a gram-negative 
bacterium. It is not a viral disease. It is just a bacterial disease and it 
could easily be cured or treated. If anybody has a headache or fever or 
skin rash, with oral antibiotics like cyprofloxacin, refampycin for children 
and injection crystalline penicillin, this can be treated. These are common 
antibiotics available anywhere in the market. These are less expensive 
antibiotics. So, this could easily be cured if we immediately go to hospital. 
But the death occurred because it took  them a little more time—two or 
three days—to go to hospital and, by which time, it became bacteraemia. 
That means, it entered into the blood vessels. 
Coming to the vaccination part, I would say that there is no short supply 
of this. There is sufficient vaccine here. But, at this point of time, vaccinating 
everybody is not required. Vaccination is only required to those people 
who have been engaged with the affected individuals, like the immediate 
relatives. If there are any symptoms of this disease then the people who 
258

are surrounding the patient should be vaccinated before one, two or three 
days and the people who are living in mass areas like hostels or jails 
where they live together without much hygiene, they should be immunised. 
So, general public need not be immunised and that is not necessary as it 
is today. As far as Haryana is concerned, the Haryana Government has 
put it on alert as it shares border with Delhi. It is good on their part to take 
preventive steps. 
The increase in the number of patients, reflects suspected cases, 
yesterday, the number of cases was 91; today it is 111. Yesterday there 
were 14 deaths; today there are 15 deaths. We are concerned about each 
and every single death. That's our concern. We don't want anybody to die. 
We are watching the situation very closely. 
Hon. Member, Shri Jairam Ramesh, has asked about the causes in the 
Capital. Sir, this bacteria, Neisseria meningococcal, is prevalent in about 
15-20 per cent of all the individuals in the pharynx, in the larynx and in the 
upper respiratory tract throughout the year. But when there is a conducive 
atmosphere, there is an outbreak. The bacteria goes to the brain and it 
become meningitis. If it goes down in the body, it becomes 
meningococcaemia. And, .neningococcaemia is even more potent. There 
are a lot of kits that are readily available. The National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases has put a lot of kits. These kits have been supplied 
to all the municipal workers, all the doctors, and all the hospitals. It is very 
easy to detect this disease. We are trying to evaluate the sensitive hot 
spots. The WHO is assisting us to evaluate that. There are more incidents 
of cases in the old city because it is very congested and lacks hygiene 
and sanitation. This disease is, in fact, transmitted through a droplet. 
When you cough there is a droplet. When you go near a patient, it is not 
that the droplet is prevalent at some point of time. Since it is a bacterium, 
it is very vulnerable. It is a very hi ghly sensitive bacterium. It does not 
remain there in the air for a long time. So, people need not panic about 
that. 
So far as preventive measures are concerned, both the Delhi Government 
and the Central Government are living up to the situation. Today also we 
had a high-level meeting at about 12.30 P.M. All the officials had attended 
the meeting. It is not that we had a meeting today only, rather we are 
having a meeting everyday. We are closely reviewing the situation so that 
it does not get out of control. We are putting it in the newspapers, we are 
putting it on the television for the public as to how to be careful. If they 
have some headache or fever, they should consult a doctor immediately. 
Unlike the other viruses, this can easily be treated.

SHRI VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY): Now, we take 
up the National Commission for the Aged Bill, 2001. Dr. Karan Singh. 
DR. KARAN SINGH (NCT OF DELHI): Sir, I move:— 
"That the Bill to provide for securing a life with dignity, peace and 
security to the aged and for their welfare and for matters connected 
therewith, be taken into consideraton." 
Sir, in our tradition, we have a well-established principle that looking 
after elderly parents is considered to be an act of great merit, a great 
punya: िजन मात-िपता की सेवा की, तीन तीथर्-ĭत िकयो न िकया, 
meaning, if somebody who has looked after his parents, it doesn't 
matter whether he has done extensive pilgrimages or kept fasts; he 
has fulfilled his karma. This is something built into our tradition. 
However, I would like to draw your attention, Sir, to the fact the di 
Sankaracharya, writing 1400 years ago in one of his strotas, has a very 
telling verse: 
 
 यावत ् िव×तोपाजर्नसक्त: तावत ् िनज पिरवारो रक्त: 
 
  पæचात जीवित जजर्र देहे वातार्ं कोिडप न पृचछित गेहे । । 
meaning, as long as you have wealth, everydody asks about our welfare, 
दादाजी कै से हɇ, नानाजी कै से हɇ ?  but once you become old and poor, 
nobody bothers about you any longer. If this was happening at the time 
of the Adi Sankara, it meant that both things continued in our society. 
There was a strong feeling that you should look after the parents; but 
there must also have been cases in which parents were grossly neglected 
and mistreated. 
Now, Sir, with the inevitable break-up of the joint family and the emergence 
of the nuclear family, the position of elders has become more precarious 
than before.The joint family, with all its shortcomings and weaknesses, 
nonetheless, did provide some kind of a security network for those who 
were elderly and for those who were incapacitated. But, now, with the 
families breaking up, and the responsibilities coming directly on the children, 
the situation is beginning to change. Many hon. Members in this House 
must have seen recently a film called Baghban where Amitabh Bachchan 
and a colleague of ours in the Rajya Sabha portrayed an elderly couple 
and the way their children treated them. That is a film that everybody 
should see because it carries within it, in a very dramatic, in a very moving 
manner, the way in which elderly people now are thirsting for affection and

are often not able to get it. 
Sir, elderly people face a whole barrage of problems. They face financial 
insecurity because, very often, they are not in pensionable jobs. It is not 
always possible for them to be insured. Therefore, they are dependent 
upon their children or upon their relatives, and financial security is something 
that strikes at the very root of dignity and of self-respect. They face physical 
insecurity. The hon. Members are aware that the crimes against elderly 
people have increased. Even in Delhi, in the Capital city we have so many 
crimes against elderly people. Elderly couples are clubbed to death; 
sometimes by servants; sometimes by  other anti-social elements. So, 
that is something also which is a matter of great concern for them. They 
are targeted because they are more vulnerable. 
Sir, as far as healthcare for the elderly people is concerned, now, there 
is a whole new branch of medicine called Gerontology. Gerontology deals 
with those problems specifically which are faced by people, as they grow 
old. As the body grows older, certain problems develop. And above all, Sir, 
it is the psychological insecurity which is the most dangerous because 
psychologically the elders do not want pity. They want dignity; they want 
their self-respect. And if that is denied to them, then, it becomes a very 
painful situation. So, whether it is financial security, physical security, 
healthcare, psychological security, it is very important that special measures 
should be taken. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, demographically, it is estimated that six per 
cent of India's population is over 60 years of age. Six per cent of India's 
population means six crores of people. Half of them are women. Therefore, 
we have this huge problem, a huge backlog. Sir, if this gentleman would 
not pass in front of me, I would be very grateful, (Interruptions) Six times 
he has passed in front of me. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY): Do not cross in 
front of the hon. Member who is speaking. You kindly take your seat. I will 
tell you later on. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: In fact, he might be interested in what I am saying 
rather than... Sir, this whole question is, the elderly people in this country 
face multiple problems. In our country, we have not yet developed a network 
of old-age homes. Old-age homes are really for the poor and destitute. 
But, in other countries, there are retirement homes for the elderly. Old-age 
homes are only for the people who are totally destitute, who cannot feed 
themselves. They live there till the end of their lives. But, there are retirement

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2 005] 
homes for the elderly, where people are prepared to pay a modest amount 
provided they can live in comfort and in security. That tradition has not yet 
developed in our country. And, I would suggest, Sir, that NGOs should be 
encouraged to undertake these sorts of ventures. There are organisations 
like Helpage India.Rotary, Lions Club and so on. 
Sir, religious trusts have vast sums of money at their disposal, and they 
should really be the pioneers in this. Let me give you the example of the 
Sikh community, which runs free l angars always. You will never see a 
Sikh beggar on the road because the Sikh community is a community 
which is full of self-respect. They have arrangements whereby elderly people 
are looked after. Or, you take the Parsi community in Mumbai and 
elsewhere. They have their trusts and they can look after them. But, these 
represent only a very small fraction  of the population of our country. 
Unfortunately, the bulk of the population is not covered either by governmental 
schemes or by NGOs and religious trusts. Therefore, something urgently 
needs to be done to look into these problems of the elderly. 
Sir, it is true that the Budget has  provided some concessions to the 
elderly, as far as taxes are concerned and travel and so on are concerned. 
But, very much more needs to be done the United Nations adopted in 
1991 what they called the U.N. Princi ples for Older Persons, and they 
urged all national Governments to include them in their programmes. There 
are many principles. But there are five particularly, to which I would like to 
draw the attention of the hon. House. Independence: Older persons should 
have access to food, water, shelter, clothing, health care, work and other 
income generating opportunities, education, training and life-enhancing 
environment. Participation: Older person should remain integrated into the 
community life and participate actively in formulation of policies affecting 
the well-being of the nation. Care: Older person should have the access to 
social, legal services and to health care so that they maintain optimum 
level of physical, mental and emotional well-being. This should include full 
respect for dignity, beliefs, needs and privacy. Self-fulfilment: Older person 
should have access to education, cultural, spiritual and rcreational resourcs 
and be able to develop their full potential. And, finally, dignity: Older person 
should be able to live in dignity and security and be free from exploitation 
and physical or mental abuse and be treated fairly regardless of age, 
gender, social or ethnic background.

Sir, elderly people have a wealth of experience. If they can be involved in civic 
affair, if their experience can be used, if they can get a sense, that they can no 
longer be thrown aside by the society, but they still continue to play a. useful 
role in the society, that will go a very long way in ameliorating their 
position. 
We have national Commissions on almost all under-privileged and special case-
groups in this country. We have the National Commission for Scheduled 
Castes, we have the National Commission for the Scheduled Tribes, we have the 
national Commission for Women and we have the National Commission for 
Minorities. We even have the National Commission for Animals. But we do not have 
a National Commission for the Aged. What I have suggested in my Bill-this Bill 
has been pending for four years. I do not know how many Lok Sabhas have 
changed in this process, but this Bill was in the pipeline and I consider it very 
fortunate that at long last, this Bill has come up. All of us are four years older than 
we were since the time I introduced the Bill, but it has, at last, come and I would 
very warmly urge the Government; the Minister is here, and the Members of the 
House are here; I would urge the Government to seriously consider setting up a 
National Commission for the Aged so that the whole host of problems that are 
being faced by elderly people in the country, to whom we owe a great deal-after all, 
if elders were not there, the youngsters would not be there— to whom we owe a 
great of debt, to whom the society owes a debt; their welfare can be looked 
after and furthered. 
With these words, I commend my Bill to the House.

some of the problems that Dr. Karan Singh has raised in his speech would

Sir, the second point I want to make is that the problems of widows in

also from a social point of view. One has to just go to Brindavan, which is

have been done in the last few years on the fate, on the social and economic 
conditions of widows. Why widowhood, is, particularly, an object of sort of 
isolation in our society, goes into history, goes into culture, which I don't 
want to get into, but the fact is t hat we have a very large proportion of 
widows living virtually without, as I said, either any family support or any 
form of social assistance, virtually, as destitutes. And, this population is 
very large, particularly, in the Nort hern part of the country. So, I think, 
when we address the problem of the aged, I think we need to look at the 
problem of widows much more carefully, and in a much more structured 
manner than we have done in the past. We have a tendency to put all of 
this as a problem of the aged, but within the aged, my own feeling is, the 
problem of widows is far more acute than we have been able to recognise 
so far. 
Sir, the third point I want to make in the context of the Bill that Dr. Karan 
Singh has put forward and the issues that he has raised, more importantly, 
in the speech that he made while introducing the Bill is the fact that when 
you are looking at the problems of the social security, quite clearly, there 
are a large number of schemes that successive Governments have come 
up with. State Governments also have their own plethora of social security 
schemes, like, maternity benefits, old-age scheme, accident-relief 
schemes, etc. So, there are a large number of schemes in Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu. Particularly, the Southern States have been pioneers in this regard,

need to address ourselves on the questions, not so much on the National 
Commission on the Aged, the need for it is incontrovertible, but how it is 
going to be structured, who is going to man this National Commission,

its mandate, etc. These are some of the more important questions that

traditional rights. This Ministry has pr epared a draft "The Scheduled Tribes

recognition of forest rights of the forest dwelling scheduled tribes, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries, including the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests.

of forest land, which they have been traditionally inhabiting for ages have not 
been adequately recognized under the existing rules and guidelines. The 
proposed Bill, therefore, seeks to recognize such rights on land, minor forest 
produce, etc. for bpnafide livelihood needs of the forest dwe lling Scheduled

established procedure taking views and comments of the stakeholder Ministries, 
including Ministry of Environment & Forest into consideration

(a) the details of the facilities provided to the children, for their career

(b) the number of the children awarded during the last five years alongwith the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) and (b) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The National Bravery Awards for children were instituted by the Indian 
Council for Child Welfare in 1957. The Indian Council for Child Welfare was 
registered as a non-government organisation under the Societies Registration 
Act XXI of 1860 on 5th June, 1952. The Awards are presented by the Hon'ble 
Prime Minister of India prior to Republic Day every year. The Awardees 
subsequently participate in the Republic Day parade. Prominent social 
workers, representatives of NGOs and re presentatives of various Government 
Departments form part of the Selection Committee. 
ICCW has taken the initiative to intr oduce a number of benefits for the 
Awardees' development and career progression with the active support and 
cooperation of the Government of India. These include the following: 
†Origirtal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Prema 
Canappa. 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
(i) The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare reserves seats in MBBS 
(maximum of two in a year) 
(ii) The Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of 
Education reserves seats in Diploma and Degree courses in 
Engineering (maximum three each in a year) for the Awardees. 
(iii) The Ministry of Railways provides free rail travel facilities upto 18 
years of age. 
In addition ICCW provides the following facilities for the development of the 
Awardees. 
(iv) Eligible Awardees are granted financial assistance for their school 
education under ICCW's Sponsorship programme. The criteria is that 
the total family income of the Awardee should not exceed Rs.2500/-
per month. 
(v) In the case of posthumous Awardees, there is a provision to provide 
Sponsorship assistance to a school going sibling if eligible under the 
Sponsorship programme of ICCW. 
(vi) Scholarship is provided for higher education such as graduation, 
engineering, medicine. 
(b) Number of Awardees from 2000 to 2004 (last five years) is 114. 
Facilities being provided to them are as detailed above according to their age, 
course of study and eligibility.

Contribution of women in public life 
*637. SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the contribution of the women political elite to national life has 
been assessed by the National Commission for Women through a study by the 
Shivaji University, Kolhapur; 
(b) the recommendations of the study report on the subject of reservations for 
women in the legislature; and 
(c) Government's view on these recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) The National Commission for Women (NCW) has 
conducted a research study on the subject: 'Contribution of Women in Political 
Elite: Implications for Women's Empowerment'through the Centre for Women's 
Studies, ShivajiUniversity, Kolhapur, Maharashtra. The main recommendations 
of the study are given in the Statement. (See below) 
(c) The National Common Minimum Programme of the Government has stated 
that the Government will take the lead to introduce legislation for one-third 
reservation for women in the House of the People and the Legislative 
Assemblies of the States. 
Statement 
Recommendations relating to reservation for women contained in the 
research study on the subject: 'Contribution of Women in Political 
Elite: Implications for Women's Empowerment' commissioned by 
the National Commission for Women 
(1) Reservations per se do not guarantee effective participation of 
women. Special efforts are required for equipping women to perform 
elective roles. Political parties must gear up their machinery towards 
fresh recruitment drives and rigorous training processes for women. 
(2) Wider public debate must be initiated and encouraged in order to develop 
a clear understanding of various complex issues involved in this policy 
of reservations. 
44 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(3) It should be made obligatory on all political parties to amend their 
constitutions in order to provide for 33% reservation for women at every 
level and in every wing of party organisations. 
(4) Minimum Common Agenda for women must be chalked out. Efforts 
should be made to see that all women representatives commit 
themselves to this agenda and lobby for pushing it forwarded within their 
own party as well as in the House, across party lines. 
(5) Constituencies reserved for women must be determined not by a draw of 
lots but by a definite sequence in rotations. This will reduce uncertainty and 
also the arbitrary element and give some breathing space to the parties 
and the aspirants. 
(6) Reservation of 1/3rd seats in various committees of Municipal 
Corporations, State Legislatures and Parliament must be provided. This will 
ensure women's exposure to all the intricacies of legislative affairs. 
(7) Women's Reservation Bill must be suitably amended in order to 
remove the drawback of the provision of rotation of reservation. 
(8) Reservations at state and nationa l level need not be an eternal 
phenomenon. The policy must be reviewed after 15 years. Fifteen years is 
a sufficient period as it will cover all the constituencies at least once. 
(9) Women's quota in party organization should be introduced and should 
stretch beyond 15 years limit. This would create a large pool of 
dynamic women candidates. 
(10) There should be reservation for women in Rajya Sabha and 
Legislative Councils as well.

Statement-II 
The steps taken by the Government to check incidents of sexual 
harassment at workplace 
* The Government has requested all the Central Ministries/ 
Departments, Chief Secretaries of all the State Governments/Union 
Territory Administrations, Universities/Institutions, Central Board of 
Secondary Education, All India Council of Technical Education 
76 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to constitute complaints committees and to ensure that the guidelines 
laid down by the Supreme Court in the Vishaka case for prevention of 
sexual harassment at workplace are implemented. 
* The National Commission for Women (NCW) formulated a Code of 
Conduct for Workplace, putting down the Supreme Court's 
guidelines mentioned above in a simple manner. This has been 
circulated to State Commission s for Women, Non-Governmental 
Organisations, the apex bodies of the Corporate Sector, Public Sector 
Undertakings, Media, Ministries/Departments and other institutions. 
* The NCW has instituted a series of interactive meetings with Public Sector 
Undertakings/Banks/Universities/Educational Institutions/ 
Hotels/Media etc. to assess the extent of implementation of the 
guidelines. 
* Department of Public Enterprises issued circular in May, 1998 to all 
administrative Ministries/Departments concerned with Central Public 
Sector Establishments to direct  the Chief Executives of CPSEs 
under their administrative control for adherence and compliance of 
the Supreme Court's guidelines on prevention of sexual harassment by 
making amendments in the CDA Rules of the CPSEs. 
* A Central Committee headed by Secretary, Department of Women and 
Child Development has been constituted in the Department of Women 
and Child Development to review the implementation of the guidelines. 
During the year 2004, the Committee met on 27-7-2004. In pursuance 
of the meeting, all Ministries/Departments and State Governments/UT 
Administrations were again requested to ensure setting up of complaints 
committee and to ensure its proper functioning. 
* So far as implementation of the Supreme Court guidelines in regard to 
setting up of com plaint committee in small establishments like shops 
and call centres are concerned, section 1(3) of the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1947 applies to every establishment wherein 
100 and more workers are employed. However, appropriate 
Government may apply the provisions of the Act to any industrial 
establishment employing less than  100 persons. Since the State 
Governments are the appropriate

Government in respect of commercial establishments like shops and 
call centres, necessary instruction have been issued by the Ministry of 
Labour and Employment duri ng January, 2005 to all Labour

the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 to small 
establishments like call centres and shops in the unorganised sector. 
* The Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 have been 
amended to include sexual harassment as a misconduct. The Central 
Civil Services (Control, Classification and Appeal) Rules, 1965 have 
been amended during July, 2004 to provide that the Complaints 
Committee established in each Ministry or Department or Office for 
inquiring into complaints of sexual harassment shall be deemed to be 
the inquiry authority appointment by the disciplinary authority and 
the Complaints Committee shall hold the inquiry as far as practicable 
in accordance with the procedure laid down in these rules (i.e. the 
procedure for holding inquiry into disciplinary proceedings for award of 
a major penalty). 
* The Department of Women and Child Development is considering 
enactment of a legislation to prohibit sexual harassment of women at 
workplace.

at workplace in the private sector could constitute an offence for which a 
workman is liable for disciplinary action.

Employment during January, 2005 to all State Labour Secretaries

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (d) The extent 
National Policy on Education (NPE) implies that, up to a given level, all 
students irrespective of castes, creed, location or sex have access to education 
of a comparable quality. It includes a common educational structure, a national 
curriculum framework and minimum levels of learning for each stage of 
education. 
Free and compulsory education for all children in the 6-14 year age group 
is now a Fundamental Right under Article-21-A of the Constitution. The enabling 
legislation to enforce the Right is currently under formulation. Once enacted, this 
legislation would provide the supporting statutory mechanism for the 
universalisation of elementary education. 
. Although the objective of universalisation of Elementary Education is yet to 
be achieved, in order to plan for the future needs for universalisation of education 
of uniform quality, Committees of the Central Advisory Board of Education have 
been set up on the subject of "Universalisation of Secondary Education" and 
"Girls Education and the Common School System". However, further steps on 
these issues would have to be based on wide consultations with the State 
Governments/UT Administrations, taking into account; the varying situation in 
the different States, the priorities of the various competing sectors and the availability 
of necessary resources. 
As regards higher education, the University Grants Commission, which is a 
statutory body, is responsible for the coordination, determination and 
maintenance of standards of university education. The AII India Council for 
Technical Education, which is also a statutory body, coordinates development 
of technical education, promotion of qualitative improvement in relation to 
quantitative growth and maintenance of norms and standards. The Government is 
committed to ensuring that these bodies, the universities as well as the institutions 
of higher learning and professional education provide quality education while

Action for violations of the codes can be taken by any authorized officer i.e. SDM, DM or 
Commissioner of Police or any other officer notified in the official gazette by the Central 
Government or State Government. 
The Central Government has constituted two inter-ministerial committee under Section 20 
of the Cable TV Networks (Regulation) Act 1995 to look into the violation of the Programme 
and Advertising Code. The Committee also takes cognizance of such violations suo-
moto. 
The Government has decided to set up a Broadcasting Regulatory Authority to 
receive and dispose of complaints on content on TV channels. A Core Group has already 
been set up in the Ministry to deliberate and draft the Bill in this regard. 
Press in India is free from Government control. The Press Council of India (PCI) is a 
statutory authority established for preserving the freedom of the Press and for maintaining and 
improving the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India. PCI has set the Norms for 
Journalists Conduct according to which Newspapers/Journalists shall not publish anything 
which is obscence, vulgar or offensive to public good taste or which has a tendency to 
malign or hurt the religious sentiments of any community or any section of society. 
The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films in accordance 
with the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules and Guidelines issued thereunder. While 
certifying films the CBFC ensures that anti-social activities, violence, sexual scenes, 
vulgarity, scenes glorifying or justifying drinking and smoking etc. are not shown. 
While certifying the 
115 

RAJYA SABHA 19 May, 2005] 
advertisements it is ensured that no visuals or words contemptuous of racial, 
religious or other groups are shown. 
Action is also taken under the existing provisions of Cable Television Networks 
(Regulation) Act, 1995 and uplinking Guidelines to regulate objectionable content of 
television channels. Recently uplinking and transmission of one television channel 
was suspended for 30 days for telecasting an objectionable movie. Show Cause Notices have 
been issued to few channels for telecasting objectionable music video. Notices have also 
been issued to a number of other channels for violating the Programme Code prescribed 
under the Cable Act. 
(b) to (d) As informed by the Ministry of External Affairs the Government is aware that an 
organization by the name of American Hindus Against Defamation has taken up the 
issues relating to printing photos of Hindu deities and religious symbols on 
undergarments of women and making the same available on the internet with a U.S.

turn consult Indian associations/ prominant NRIs and then take up the issue appropriately 
with the local Government/organizations.

Tata-Star DTH venture 
4871. SHRI ABANl ROY: 
SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to media reports on 
"Tata-Murdoch DTH venture clearance"; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether his Ministry has delayed grant of license to Tata-Star Direct-To-
Home (DTH) venture inspite of FDI approval and acceptance of requisite license 
fee; and 
(d) whether Government propose to hold a joint meeting of the concerned 
Ministries to thresh out the case of Tata-Star DTH venture immediately and if 
not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The application of M/s. Space TV is under examination. 
Issues of Space T.V. 
4872. SHRIMATI KAMLA MANHA R: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are examining various issues of Space T.V., the 
Direct To Home (DTH) joint venture with Tata Sons before issue of licence; 
(b) if so, the details of the points being examined by the Department of 
Company Affairs (DCA); 
(c) whether most of the issues being examined by DCA have already been 
examined by the Ministry of Finance at the time of giving clearances of their FDI 
proposal; and 
(d) if so, the reasons for reexamination of same issues by the DCA? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir.

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
(b) This Ministry had sought the comments/Views of the Ministry of 
Company Affairs on certain provisions contained in Shareholders' Agreement 
among M/s. Space TV, M/s. Tata Sons and M/s. Network Digital Distribution

(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise. 
Implementation of CAS 
4873. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have been approached by the cable operators to re-
consider implementation of the Conditional Access System (CAS); 
(b) if so, the details of their demands; 
(c) what about the pay-channel factor; and 
(d) to what extent Government are prepared to accede to the request of the 
cable operators while protecting interest of the subscribers? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (d) This Ministry has initiated consultative process with 
all the stake holders including the cable operators, to examine TRAI's 
recommendations on "issues relating to broadcasting and distribution of TV 
channels". The Cable Operators Federation of India (COFI) had requested the Ministry 
for a meeting to discuss their concerns including the implementation of 
Conditional Access System. This meeting was held on 28.4.2005. The 
Government would take a final decision after consultation with all stakeholders 
and requisite inter ministerial consultation on TRAI's recommendations.

INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken by Government to curb growing influence of the 
Corporate House in Government's decision making process; 
(b) whether it is a fact that a busin essman and an executive of a big 
corporate house were involved in a deal with Doordarshan;

various deals; and

controversial corporate executive? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (d) Decisions on various matters relating to the 
Information and Broadcasting Sector are taken in accordance with prescribed 
rules and procedures. While no outside interference is countenanced, Prasar 
Bharati have also informed that in the absence of specific question, it is not 
possible for them to offer comments. 
Obscenity on TV channels 
4875. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the increasing incidences of indiscriminate beaming of 
obsence scenes on television corrupts impressionable minds and embarrasses 
family audiences; 
(b) whether to check this menace, Government propose to enact a new law to 
ban such beaming over electronic media; 
(c) whether towards this an autonomous broadcasting authority is proposed 
to be set up, on the lines of Federal Communication Commission in the United 
States; and 
(d) whether the jurisdiction of such a regulatory body would also extend to 
display of visuals through cellular phone channels? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (d) Government is contemplating the establishment of an 
autonomous Authority to regulate content on television channels. Such 
Authorities exist in many countries. FCC in USA is one such authority. The details 
of a draft legislation are being worked out.

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has gone through the Report released jointly by the 
National Commission for women and the Press Institute of India which says 
that majority of the women journalists are discriminated against by men at work 
places; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by his Ministry to rectify the situation? . 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Main recommendations of the report are given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) Action on the recommendations is to be taken by various Ministries/ 
Departments including Ministry of Labour and Employment, National 
Commission for Women, Ministry of Human Resource Development, Press 
Council of India and the newspaper houses. 
Statement 
Main Recommendations of the Report 
Gender sensitisation 
* Gender sensitisation both for men and women. This can be done through 
the Press Academy in Hyderabad in collaboration with the NCW and 
PII for other parts of the country. 
* Introduction of gender writing in journalism courses with a threefold 
objective—to view language, understand issues concerned and to help 
journalists' to learn to deal with gender issues. NCW could work with 
the University Grants Commission to deal with this issue. 
* Gender-sensitisation courses especially at under-graduate level. 
154 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* There should be uniform conditions for leave, wage increase for men 
and women. 
* A difference can be made to media output by giving thought to 
gender differentiation and bringing equity to the workplace. 
Training 
* Enthusiasm often watered down by unresponsive organizations that are 
not sensitive to gender specific requirements which are often viewed 
as liabilities. 
* A male journalist is often given guidance by an experienced senior 
male colleague on entering the profession. Women journalists have no 
such apprenticeship. 
* Training and information sessions are a must to confidently operate in 
the environment and also to change mindsets. 
* Women journalists should be trained on how to negotiate contracts, 
this can be done by the NUJ/DUJ etc. so that women journalists 
know what they are entitled to. There should be transparency in policy 
matters. 
* Periodic upgradation of skills, knowledge and technology. 
* Encourage people to take sabbaticals. 
* Encourage more lateral movement and recognise contribution to 
check stagnation. 
* Regional Press should encourage women into hard reporting-politics, 
mainstream, production etc. so that promotions are easier. 
* Regular training, re-orientation. 
* Efforts to combat frustration on the desk. 
* Zero tolerance should become the norm, pushed by organizations. 
* Performance based promotions based on periodic appraisal. 
Working conditions 
* Basic facilities should be provided in offices as per requirements 
of women employees, especially toilets and canteen. 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
* Women should be appointed at the top level management, they might 
be able to help other women. 
* There should be some rules and regulations to maintain discipline in 
organizations. 
* Transfer should not be used to victimise women journalists. 
* Food facilities should be provided  during overtime, or night shift 
because women are unable to go out and have dinner at hotel/ dhabas 
in the night. 
* Packed dinner should be served on night shifts. 
Sexual harassment 
* NCW should run campaigns on sexual harassment. NCW could have 
an interactive session with media managements on how to identify 
sexual harassment cases. 
* A complaint box could be introduced in view of the Supreme Court 
decision on the Vishaka case. While each organization should have 
its own box, others could have a box at their respective press 
academies—where they exist. 
* Since cells have not been set up in most newspaper organizations the 
Government should re-issue the circular. 
* Newspaper organizations should report to the NCW on the 
progress of setting up these cells. 
* NCW should ask all newspaper orga nizations to report about the 
formation and constitution of the cells and list out its members. 
* Ombudsperson to look into sexual harassment cases. 
* Could a cell be set up in the Press Council to hear specifically about 
issues related to women journalists—such as their transfers, 
promotions, nightshirts, maternity leave, special needs and sexual 
harassment etc.

(b) and (c) The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films in

be so designed as to conform to the laws of the country and should not offend 
morality, decency and religious susceptibilities of the subscribers. The Central 
Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial Committee under Section 20 
of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 to look into the violations 
of the Programme and Advertising Code. The enforcement of both the 
Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the Cable Networks Regulation Act, 1995 lies 
with the State Governments.

  Statement-III  
The steps taken by Government for eradication of illiteracy among Scheduled 
Castes 
Education is in the Concurrent List of the Constitution and school education is 
primarily the responsibility of State Governments. The Central Government, on 
its part, supports various initiatives of the State Govern-ments. The Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) and its components, District Prirary Education 
Programme (DPEP), National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary 
Education (NPNSPE), Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBVs), Mahila 
Samakhya (MS), National Programme for Education of Girls at Elementary 
Level (NPEGEL), Shiksha Karmi Project (SKP) are some of the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes for supporting the initiatives taken by the State Governments 
to provide education to children in the age group 6-14 years besides 
mainstreaming out-of-school children and dropouts. Some interventions aimed at 
bringing into the mainstream to the children from the socially weaker sections 
of society are: 
* Relaxed norms for opening of primary/Middle schools in SC 
habitations. 
* Abolition of tuition fee in all States in Government Schools at least 
upto the upper primary level. 
* Incentives like free textbooks, uniforms, stationery, school bags, 
scholarships, opening of alternative schooling facilities in unserved 
180 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
habitations, trainging of community leaders with the objectives to 
mobilize SC communities for enrolment of their children, bridge 
courses/remedial teaching, engagement of teachers from local 
communities, construction of hostels for SC boys and girls, etc. 
* SCs are given 15% reservation in Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs) and 
Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVs). 
* Department of Elementary Educa tion and Literacy has earmarked 
notionally Rs. 900 crore for SCP out of the plan outlay of Rs. 6000 
crore for Annual Plan 2004-05. 
* The Government of India has launched National Literacy Mission to 
eradicate adult illiteracy. 
* Programmes are broadcast/telecast in Hindi and Regional Languages 
for spreading awareness ab out the various welfare 
Schemes/Literacy Programmes of the Government. Awareness is also 
spread through print media.

Tribal artisans under new WTO regime 
4911. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the traditional tribal artisans would be protected under new WTO 
regime; 
(b) whether Government are considering to unveil a new tribal welfare policy 
to address the concerns of the tribals; and 
(c) the protection being provided to ensure that tribal people would not be 
uprooted from their traditional vocations under the new trade regime? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (c) 
As indicated by the Ministry of Commerce, under the provisions of the TRIPS 
Agreement of WTO, protection is provided to seven categories of intellectual 
property rights, viz. copyright and related rights, patents, geographical 
indications, trademarks, industrial designs, layout-designs of integrated circuits 
and undisclosed information. In addition, protection is also provided to new 
plant varieties. Works of traditional tribal artisans are prior art and their traditional 
knowledge fall under public domain and therefore these do not belong to any of the 
above seven categories of intellectual property rights. As such, at present no 
protection is available to works of traditional tribal artisans as well as their 
traditional knowledge under the TRIPS Agreements of WTO. 
Tribal Co-operative Marketing Development Federation of India Limited 
(TRIFED) is running a tribes shop for marketing tribal arts and crafts for 
benefit of scheduled tribes artisans. 
The Department of Culture, Ministry of Tourism and Culture also implement a 
scheme of "Promotion and Dissemination of tribal/Folk Art and Culture" 
which covers the well-identified and urgent need for the preservation, promotion 
and dissemination of tribal art and culture.

4918. SHRI NABAM REBIA: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether ownership of tribals over Minor Forest Produce (MFP) is being 
given due recognition by Government; 
(b) if so, the details of Government's policy in this regard; and 
(c) the role of the Panchayats therein? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (c) 
Yes, Sir. The provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) 
Act, 1996 (PESA, 1996), enacted by the Government, gives the rights of 
ownership of Minor Forest Produce (MFP) to the Panchayats at the appropriate 
level and the respective Gram Sabhas. Each State Government is, therefore, 
required to amend its Panchayati Raj Act to incorporate the provisions of PESA. 
The Ministry has asked the State Governments to confer ownership rights in 
respect of minor forest produce (MFP), including tendu patta, on the Scheduled 
Tribes are providing definition of MFP, which should be all the traditional 
produce being produced by all the tribals, by amending the concerned State 
Legislations, as provided in the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the 
Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996. The Ministry of Environment & Forests has also 
drafted a Model "State Minor Forest Produce (Ownership of Forest Dependent 
Community) Bill, 2004" for conferring ownership right of MFP on local 
communities.

Sub.:  Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in townships, housing, built-up

With a view to catalysing investment in townships, housing, built-up 
infrastructure and construction-development projects as an instrument to generate 
economic activity, create new employment opportunities and add to the 
available housing stock and built-up infrastructure, the Government has 
decided to allow FDI up to 100% under the automatic route in townships, 
housing, built-up infrastructure and construction-development projects (which 
would include, but not be restricted to, housing, commercial premises, hotels, 
resorts, hospitals, educational instituti ons, recreational facilities, city and 
regional level infrastructure), subject to the following guidelines; 
(a) Minimum area to be developed under each project would be as under:

(i) In case of development of serviced housing plots, a minimum land 
area of hectares. 
(ii) In case of construction-development projects, a minimum built-up 
area of 50,000 sq. mts. 
(iii) In case of a combination pr oject, any one of the above two 
conditions would suffice. 
(b) the investment would further be subject to the following conditions: 
(i) Minimum capitalization of US $ 10 million for wholly owned 
subsidiaries and US $ 5 million for joint ventures with Indian 
partners. The funds would have to be brought in within six months of 
commencement of business of the Company. 
(ii) Original investment cannot be repatriate before a period of three years 
from completion of minimum capitalization. However, the investor 
may be permitted to exit earlier with prior approval of the 
Government through the FIPB. 
(c) At least 50 of the project must be developed within a period of five years 
from the date of obtaining all statutory clearances. The investor would not be 
permitted to sell undeveloped plots. For the purpose of these guidelines, 
"undeveloped plots" will mean where roads, water supply, street lighting, drainage, 
sewerage, and other conveni ences, as applicable under prescribed regulations, 
have not been made available. It will be necessary that the investor provides this 
infrastructure and obtains the completion certificate from the concerned local 
body/service agency before he would be allowed to dispose of serviced housing 
plots.

use requirements and provision of community amenities and common facilities,

other regulations of the States Government/Municipal/Local Body concerned.

including those of the building/layout plans, developing internal and peripheral 
areas and other infrastructure facilities, payment of development, external 
development and other charges and complying with all other requirements as 
prescribed under applicable rules/bye-laws/regulations of the State 
Govemment/Municipal/Local Body concerned.

Revision of poverty alleviation targets 
4945. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have revised the target set for the Tenth Five Year 
Plan regarding alleviation of poverty prevailing in the cities; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to achieve the target set under such programme 
alongwith the success achieved in relation thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN EMPLOY-
MENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) to (c) The • 
Tenth Five Year Plan period (2002—2007) has set a target for reduction of poverty 
by 5 percentage points by the year 2007 and by 15 percentage points by 2012. 
The Tenth Plan does not specify any separate targets for reducing poverty levels 
in cities. 
In the urban areas, Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation is 
implementing an employment oriented Urban Poverty Alleviation Programme 
named Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), on all India basis, 
through States/Union Territories, with effect from 01.12.1997. The scheme 
envisages to provide gainful employment to the urban unemployed and 
underemployed poor .through, firstly, encouraging the setting up of self-
employment ventures by those who have studied upto 9th standard and, secondly, 
by providing wage employment by utilizing their labour for construction of 
socially and economically useful public assets. 
220 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
During the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—07), on all India basis, targets to 
provide 4,00,000 employment opportunities to the urban poor, through setting up 
of micro/group enterprises and to impart skill training to 5,00,000 persons have 
been fixed under SJSRY. During the first three years of the Tenth Plan, i.e. from 
2002-2003 to 2004-2005, comulatively, 2,97,419 micro-enterprises have been set up 
and 3,27,399 urban poor have been provided skill training.

Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993" by all the

their dependents (NSLRS) envisages financial assistance to scavengers for their 
training and rehabilitations in alternate dignified occupations.

and Empowerment to M/o Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation, Rs. 
34.97 crores of total Central assistance (Rs. 21.41 crores in 2003-04 and Rs. 
13.56 crores in 2004-05) was released for training of 5649 scavengers and 
rehabilitation of 26721 scavengers.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Situation arising out of the large scale devastation caused by 
Tsunami on 26th December, 2004. 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, in this august House, we are 
discussing an unexpected human tr agedy, which occurred on 26th 
December. At the outset, I would pay homage to thousands of victims who lost 
their lives in this unexpected tragedy. 
Sir, tsunami is a new kind of natural calamity, which we never faced before in 
our country. I have had the opportunity to visit some of the tsunami-affected areas. Of 
course, not only me, right from the Prime Minister to a good number of Union 
Cabinet Ministers, social activists, State Ministers and MPs had also visited and 
extended all kinds of support to victims of this tragedy. While we are discussing 
this tsunami issue, there are two things that we have to discuss seriously. 
One issue is the failure in assessing the situation and to provide sufficient 
warnings, which would have been more helpful to extend rescue work. Sir, it 
was reported that when tsunami tidal waves started in the eastern part of Asia, 
the U.S. Tsunami Warning Centre at Los Angeles had detected the arrival of tsunami, 
248 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
but it did not know whom to inform about it in India. It means that we do 
not have a system to assess this kind of seismic problems. So, this is the 
important issue, which we have to discuss. 
Wny did it happen? We have developed science and technology; we 
have developed atmosphere and ocean sciences; and our country also 
claims that we have the third largest number of scientific community in the 
world. Only day before yesterday, we complimented our scientific 
community in this House. Till now, we do not know why we failed to given 
sufficient warning to the people. This was an international tragedy. In our 
country, it occurred first in the Andamans, then after six hours, it came to 
Tamil Nadu, and then another two hours later, it came to Kerala. We were 
not in a position to provide sufficient warnings to our poor people who were 
staying in coastal areas. Had we been able to given sufficient warning, we 
would have been in a position to evacuate larger number of population. 
This is an experience, which we gained. At a later date when we got the 
information about tsunami again from the Central Government, the Ministry 
of Science and Technology, people were evacuated. Nothing happened 
because now a system was there. It wa s all due to the initiative of the 
Government. Once a tragedy occurred, then from that experience, we can 
give warning and do rescue work in future. That is possible. Why I am 
discussing this matter here in this House, because we have a failure in 
this country not only in the case of tsunami but also in all kinds of natural 
calamities that have occurred, whether tornado or any such incident. We 
do not have a system to protect our people. If such kind of natural calamity 
as this takes place in the Western countries, they are able to evacuate 
their people. They will be able to save the lives of the common men. In 
India,'so far, we do not have any such devices to protect or evacuate our 
general public from the natural calamities even though we do get sufficient 
information in advance. So, from the experience of tsunami, what the 
Government is going to do with regard to developing a system in our country

SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR (P unjab): Sir, NABARD plays an 
important role in providing agricultural credit to the farmers. At present, it 
provides refinance for agricultural credit to the tune of 30 per cent of such 
credit advanced by the Cooperative Banks in the States at the rate of 5.25 
per cent. On the other hand, primary agricultural cooperative societies are 
advancing agricultural credit @ 11 per cent, after raising funds from the 
Central Cooperative Banks. To augment the agricultural credit facilities for 
farmers at affordable rates of interest, the Government of Punjab has re-
quested NABARD to increase the refinance limit from 30 per cent to 70 
per cent and to reduce the rate of interest from 5.25 per cent to 3 per cent 
so as to enable the Cooperative Banks to advance agricultural credit to 
farmers @ 9 per cent. NABARD had hitherto been providing subsidy up to 
25 per cent for construction of rural godowns for the want of which the

w.e.f. October 1, 2004. Since the fa rmers continue to suffer enormous 
damage to foodgrains and other farm products for want of storage, this 
scheme would be allowed to continue to help the farmers to build their 
own godowns. I would, therefore, urge upon the Government to expedite a 
decision in the matter.

Need to take steps for increasing farm Producitvity 
SHRI TARIQ ANWAR (Maharashtra): Sir, it needs no repetition that the 
agricultural sector holds an important place in the Indian economy. The 
productivity of Indian agriculture is very poor. India ranks at or near bottom 
of the list of countries in the world in terms of productivity per acre for 
almost all major crops. Although we have more arable land than China, 
India produces less than half the quantity of foodgrains grown by China. 
Brazilian yields of black pepper are six times higher than India, utilising 
varieties originally imported from India. In rice, Indian yields are one-third 
the level in North Korea. Maize yiel ds are one-sixth the level of Chile. 
Wheat yields are one-third Ireland's average. Soybean yields are one-third 
the level achieved in South Africa. Prductivity in pulses is one-tenth the 
level of France. In groundnut, Indian yields are one-sixth Israel's average. 
The average yield of tomato in India is 12 tons per acre versus 34 tons in 
the USA. Israel's food and agricultural output valued at 4 billion US dollars, 
is produced on just one million acres of very arid land. India has 400 
million acres of land at its disposal. Imagine what we can achieve with 
such productivity! 
I, therefore, urge the hon. Agriculture Minister to start a programme of 
establishing soil-testing labs across the country, which are fully capable 
of analysing the soil for all its 13 nutrients. Such a programme would also 
have to be accompanied by a training programme of district and block 
level agriculture functionaries who would have the responsibility to develop 
new techniques for growing various crops, based on the results of soil 
tests, and make suitable recommendations to the farmers.
